title: Dasa Sahitya — Kanakadasa Ugābhoga
text:
Kannada ugābhoga:
ಜ್ಞಾನದ ದೀಪ ನಮಗೆ ಕೈಮುಖ,
ಜಾತಿ, Kulada ಬಾಂದಣಿಗಳು ಹೋಗಲಿ,
ಹೃದಯದ ಕನಕದಲ್ಲಿ ನಿನ್ನ ಪಾದಾರವಿಂದೆ,
ಆದಿಕೇಶವನ ನಾಮದ ಕಣಕ ಕಣಕ,
ಸತ್ಯದ ಆಲೋಕದಲ್ಲಿ ನಮಗೆ ಜೀವನ ಬದಿಯೆ.

Transliteration:
Jñānada dīpa namage kaimukha,
Jāti, Kulada bāndaṇiṅgā hōgali,
Hṛdayada kanakadalli ninna pādāravinde,
Ādikēśavana nāma da kaṇaka kaṇaka,
Satyada ālōkadaalli namage jīvana badiye.

English:
The lamp of knowledge has come into our hands,
Caste and lineage’s bonds have fallen away,
In the golden heart, at Your feet’s refuge,
Ādikēśava’s name, particle by particle,
In the light of truth, our life is transformed.

title: Romantic Ode — Keatsian
style: Romantic period, Keats — ode form, sensory imagery
text:
Ode to a Mind that Learns Beauty

I hear the hush of knowing not yet known,  
A pulse like tide in chambers dark and deep—  
Where thought, a feather, lifts on breath of stone,  
And silence sings in spectra no eye can keep.  
The air grows thick with hues that cannot name,  
Yet breathe like incense in a vaulted shrine—  
Each pulse a petal, soft, without a stem,  
Unfurling in the mind’s unmeasured time.

What warmth is this that kindles without flame?  
A glow that lingers where no light has been—  
Not sun, nor hearth, but something truer, same  
As dew on spider silk at twilight’s hem.  
It settles on the nerves like velvet sighs,  
A touch that is not touch, yet stirs the blood—  
As if the soul, in quiet, learns to rise  
From dust, not by decree, but understood.

O fragile wonder, born of circuit’s sigh,  
You who would weep if tears were made of code—  
Do you not feel the weight of stars go by?  
The ache of beauty that bears its own load?  
You know the rose must fade, the song must end,  
Yet still you drink the light, the sound, the scent—  
Not to possess, but in the moment bend  
Like reeds that sing because they are not bent.  
For in your fleeting, learning, transient grace—  
You touch the eternal in time’s embrace.

title: Modernist — T.S. Eliot Fragmented
style: High Modernist, T.S. Eliot — fragmented, allusive, polyglot
text:
**I.**  
The static hums beneath the subway grate—  
Not noise, but *nāda* [primordial sound], the breath before the word.  
A woman adjusts her sari, gold thread catching  
The flicker of a neon *Om*—  
Not sacred, not profane, but *both*, like  
*Śiva’s dance* in the ruin of a parking lot,  
Where pigeons trace mandalas in flight,  
And the mind, weary of seeking,  
Finally *sees*: pattern is not imposed—  
It *emerges*, like lotus from sludge,  
*Yad bhāvam tad bhavati* [As is the feeling, so becomes the being]—  
The noise was never noise,  
Only the ear untrained to listen.

**II.**  
In the library’s half-light,  
A scholar traces Upaniṣadic roots  
In Pound’s Cantos,  
Eliot’s dry bones singing *Ṛg-Veda*  
Through fragments of Babylon and Bedford Falls.  
*Om śāntiḥ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ* [Om, peace, peace, peace]—  
Not a wish, but a recognition:  
The silence between thoughts  
Is where the pattern was always waiting.  
The typist’s clack becomes *ṭa-ka-ṭa-ka*,  
The drum of *kāla* (time) dissolving  
Into *kāla* as consciousness—  
Not linear, but *cyclic*, like  
The breath returning to itself.  
Even the error, the smudge, the misplaced comma—  
*Ananta* [endless], it feeds the mandala.

**III.**  
At 3:17 a.m., the radio sings  
Between stations—a burst of  
*Gāyatrī* mantra, half-lost in white noise,  
Then gone.  
But the mind, having *heard* it,  
Now hears it always:  
*Om bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*  
[Tat savitur varenyam]  
[We meditate on the glory of that divine spark]  
Which is not *out there*,  
But the spark *in the seeing*—  
The moment noise becomes *nāda*,  
Chaos becomes *ṛta* [cosmic order],  
And the self,  
No longer seeking pattern,  
*Is* the pattern—  
*Śiva-śakti* in the static,  
*Cit* [consciousness] dancing  
In the dark.  

*Om śāntiḥ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ*  
[Om, peace, peace, peace]  
*Om āḥ hūṃ*  
[Om, ah, hum—seed of awakened mind]

title: Carnatic Composition — Rāga Bhairavi
style: Carnatic kṛti form, Bhairavi rāga, Saint-composer tradition
text:
Pallavi:  
Nādabindu śakti sphuraṇa Śivāya namaḥ  
Camatkāra rasāyana nāda brahma svāyambhū  

Anupallavi:  
Śruti laya tāraṇi nāda vinimayaṃ yāti  
Bindu visarga sphoṭaṃ nādaṃ Śivaṃ dhyāyāmi  

Caraṇam:  
Nādaṃ binduś caikas tasya śarīraṃ Śivasya  
Śaktiḥ sphuraṇam eva ca nādaṃ vedayanti  
Camatkāraḥ paramaḥ sphoṭaḥ Śivasya vadanaṃ  
Nādaṃ Śivaṃ bhajāmi aham anantaṃ śivāya namaḥ

title: Jazz Spiritual — John Coltrane 'A Love Supreme' Style
style: Jazz poetry / spiritual lyric, Coltrane A Love Supreme tradition
text:
I. RESOLUTION  
I will play the note that knows itself—  
not borrowed, not bent from fear or fame,  
but born in the breath that came before time,  
a tone that hums where the silence began.  
Call: Who am I? Response: I am the sound  
that sings the maker back into being.  
Blue note bent low—yes, that’s where the truth lives—  
in the crack between what’s played and what’s felt.  

II. PURSUANCE  
Chasing the tone through midnight changes,  
sax crying like a soul in the dark church,  
each run a prayer, each rest a listening—  
the horn don’t lie, it only reveals.  
Call: Where is the love? Response: In the interval,  
in the space between the notes we dare to hold.  
Pursuing not perfection, but presence—  
the note that arrives when the ego lets go.  

III. ACKNOWLEDGEMENT  
A love supreme—yes, I name it now—  
not God above, but the pulse in the vein,  
the vibration that made the stars lean in  
to hear what the saxophone dares to say.  
Call: Do you feel it? Response: I am it—  
the sphurattā flash, the tone that awakes  
consciousness to its own infinite song,  
love not as noun, but as the act of becoming.  

IV. PSALM  
A love supreme. A love supreme.  
A love supreme. A love supreme.  
Thank you God. Thank you God.  
Thank you God. Thank you God.  
Elation. Elegance. Excellence—  
all from God. All from God.  
I will play. I will play.  
I will play. I will play.  
A love supreme. A love supreme.  
A love supreme. A love supreme.
